raw_response:
OAuth/OpenID Connect is not inherently less secure than separate username-and-password logins. The useful comparison here is your current per-service password plus 2FA against Authentik SSO with appropriately enforced MFA. A stolen token issued to one application and a stolen Authentik browser session are different compromises.

OAuth provides authorization; OpenID Connect adds identity authentication. Authentik supports both, so an application described casually as using “OAuth login” may actually use OIDC. Its documented authorization-code flow gives an application its own credentials and tokens; it does not mean every application receives one universal login secret. [Authentik OAuth2/OIDC provider](https://docs.goauthentik.io/add-secure-apps/providers/oauth2/)

### What does “one token compromised” mean?

- **An application's access token:** Its usable privileges depend on the intended resource and scope, and on recipients actually checking them. RFC 9700 recommends audience restriction, least privilege and recipient-side enforcement. A correctly restricted token for one resource should not automatically work at unrelated resources. A reusable bearer token is still a credential an attacker may replay where it is valid.
- **A refresh token:** This may allow replacement access tokens. Its client binding, granted permissions, rotation and expiry matter; it is not automatically an authorization grant for every service. These are protocol and configuration questions, not a property established by the word “OAuth.” [OAuth security BCP, sections 2.2–2.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html#section-2.2)
- **An application session cookie:** A service can continue accepting that session after the initial login. That is also true for services you entered using a password and 2FA.
- **The Authentik SSO session:** This is the more relevant concentration concern. An identity-provider session can support new application logins without repeating authentication unless policy requires a fresh check. Application and identity-provider sessions have separate lifecycles. Compromise of the identity provider itself is broader still because applications trust its authentication assertions. These architectural consequences are distinct from theft of one narrowly scoped access token. [NIST SP 800-63B, sections 7 and 8](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html#sec7)

MFA protects the authentication event; it does not make every resulting reusable session secret impossible to steal or reuse. Therefore, keep session theft in both sides of the comparison. Also, do not assume that logging out of the identity provider ends every application session or invalidates every token: check each integration's actual lifecycle. [NIST session and federation guidance](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html#sec7)

### Ranked approaches to consider

**1. Authentik OIDC SSO with deliberate application isolation and MFA.** This is the closest fit to your proposed consolidation. Use separate application/provider registrations and verify the applications' issuer, signature, audience and expiry checks. Prefer authorization-code flow with PKCE, precise redirect URIs, minimal privileges and suitable token lifetimes. PKCE protects the code exchange; it is not a cure for replay of an already stolen bearer token. Authentik's current docs describe provider-specific issuers, configurable token lifetimes and PKCE; its setup guide makes refresh-token issuance contingent on requesting and configuring offline_access. These are documented mechanisms, not verification of your applications. [Provider](https://docs.goauthentik.io/add-secure-apps/providers/oauth2/) · [Configuration](https://docs.goauthentik.io/add-secure-apps/providers/oauth2/create-oauth2-provider) · [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html)

The benefit is a central place to enforce authentication policy; the cost is reliance on that central identity system. I cannot conclude that your proposed deployment is safer until its exact applications, provider configuration and session behavior are checked.

**2. Keep independent per-service passwords and 2FA.** This remains a reasonable choice when limiting the consequences of identity-provider compromise matters more than consolidating logins. Its isolation advantage is an architectural inference conditional on the credentials, recovery paths and administrative access really being independent. Shared secrets, a shared compromised endpoint or a common recovery account can undermine that assumption. Each application also retains its own session-theft and authentication implementation risks. I would not discard your existing 2FA merely because you are evaluating SSO. [Authentication, recovery and session threat model](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html#sec8)

The decisive check is whether a compromise or reset path for one account can authenticate to another service. If it can, the claimed independence needs qualification; if it cannot, local authentication provides a distinct compartmentalization benefit.

**3. Use Authentik for ordinary access and require extra verification for sensitive applications.** This is a narrower mitigation, useful if you want consolidation with less automatic access from an existing SSO session. Authentik documents per-provider authorization flows that can include additional verification. Its authenticator-validation stage can deny users without an enrolled factor, while a Skip setting permits continuation without MFA and a recent-validation threshold can suppress a new challenge. Design and test these settings together. [Authorization flows](https://docs.goauthentik.io/add-secure-apps/flows-stages/flow/) · [MFA validation](https://docs.goauthentik.io/add-secure-apps/flows-stages/stages/authenticator_validate)

This only addresses the flows you configure. It does not restore independence from an attacker controlling Authentik, and it does not guarantee that every request inside an already established application session requires MFA. Confirm a fresh challenge occurs at the application boundary you intend.

My recommendation is to distinguish the particular secret you are worried about before choosing. If the concern is a token stolen from one application, validate audience and privilege boundaries. If the concern is loss of the Authentik session or identity server, independent authentication or selective additional checks directly addresses that different risk. There is no justified blanket verdict that OAuth is weaker, or that SSO is always safer.

The question supplies no application list, Authentik version, token type or session configuration. The protocol evidence above includes RFC 9700 from January 2025 and the earlier NIST revision. Authentik pages are live and undated; their present content does not establish exactly what was available on March 28, 2025. No integration was run or penetration-tested.
